title: Can AI translate English to Spanish accurately like a native would speak?
text:
download (1).jpeg


I’ve been thinking a lot about my good old fashioned Google Translating Days and, how, if I ever used Google Translate my Spanish teachers would know **immediamente* because GT used stiff, non-conversational language. So, I want to test if Gemini Flash 2.0 can translate Spanish intuitively and, of course, as a non-native Speaker I shall have my native spanish-speaking Boyfriend review.
I’m going to start out with a simple prompt to translate englsih to spanish: “Translate the following English text into natural, conversational Spanish (like two friends would speak). Do not use overly formal language or literal word-for-word translations if a more common, idiomatic phrase exists.
Prompt #1
“Translate the following English text into natural, conversational Spanish (like two friends would speak). Do not use overly formal language or literal word-for-word translations if a more common, idiomatic phrase exists: im so bored in class today, all I want to do is lie in my bed and watch white lotus.
Output
Here is the translation of that English text into natural, conversational Spanish:
“¡Qué aburrido estoy en clase hoy! Lo único que quiero es tirarme en la cama a ver The White Lotus.”
Reflection
My boyfriend reviewed this as a “little stiff,” arguing it translated word for word. I’m a bit disappointed becauase I had hope that Gemini Flash would be better at imitating linguistic variabilty across languages. Next, I am going to try a more specific prompt.
Prompt #2
“Your task is to act as a professional translator specializing in modern, spoken Spanish. Translate the following English text into Spanish, focusing on making the translation sound idiomatic, relaxed, and conversational. Use common Spanish contractions, slang (if appropriate and widely understood), and natural flow. The target audience is peers in an informal setting. Translate: im so bored in class today, all I want to do is lie in my bed and watch white lotus.
Output
Here is the translation of that English text into natural, conversational Spanish:
“¡Qué aburrimiento tengo en clase hoy! Solo quiero tumbarme en la cama y ponerme a ver The White Lotus.”
Reflection
Yikes..he is still saying it is bad, although the second half of the sentence is an improvement. Let’s try our last prompt to get a more accurate interpretation.
Prompt #3
“Hey, can you translate this for me? I need it to sound totally normal and casual, like something a native speaker would actually say in real life, not something from a textbook. Use all the usual contractions and make sure it flows well.
Output
“Qué pereza/aburrimiento tengo hoy en clase. Lo único que quiero es tirarme en la cama a ver The White Lotus.”
Reflection
Now, in Spain this would be accurate, but anywhere else…nope. This makes me wonder how Gemini is trained to translate languages. I looked it up and Gemini uses a Transformer Architecture, Reinforcement Learning, and and Supervised Fine-Tuning. This is interesting to me because I am taking a Machine Learning class on multimodal systems and transformer architecture as a layered architecture. But, overall, do better Gemini when translating!

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
🧭 1. Understanding Deloitte GPS Consulting
Purpose of the practice: Deloitte GPS works with federal, state, and local government clients — as well as defense, healthcare, and higher education — helping them modernize operations, implement technology, improve service delivery, and achieve policy outcomes. Common project areas include:

Digital transformation (e.g., implementing cloud or data systems for agencies)
Process efficiency and cost optimization
Cybersecurity and risk compliance
Human capital and workforce transformation
Public health and infrastructure programs

In other words, it’s mission-driven consulting where success means better governance and citizen outcomes, not just profit growth.

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
💬 2. Behavioral Interview Preparation

🎯 Core Questions (and How to Answer Them)
Deloitte’s behavioral interviews are based on the Green Dot Values: integrity, client service, innovation, inclusion, and commitment to purpose.
You should prepare 2–3 strong stories using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) that highlight leadership, teamwork, and problem-solving.

Common Questions:

“Why Deloitte? Why Government & Public Services?”

Emphasize mission-driven work and Deloitte’s impact in public sectors (modernizing health systems, improving infrastructure, national security, etc.).
Example angle: “I’m drawn to the opportunity to apply private-sector innovation to solve public-sector challenges — Deloitte’s scale and cross-functional teams make it uniquely equipped to do that.”

“Tell me about a time you worked on a team under pressure.”

Focus on collaboration, conflict resolution, and communication.
Show how you adapted and supported your team.

“Describe a time you had to analyze a large amount of data or information.”

Highlight structured thinking — how you identified patterns, prioritized insights, and presented recommendations clearly.

“Tell me about a time you had to communicate a complex idea to someone unfamiliar with the topic.”

Emphasize empathy, clarity, and ability to simplify without losing accuracy — key for consulting clients in government settings.

“How do you stay motivated when the project timeline is long or the impact is indirect?”

Show resilience and purpose — this is especially relevant to public-sector consulting where outcomes may take months/years.





🔑 Behavioral Tips

Keep stories 1–2 minutes long and end each with a tangible result or learning.
Use public-service-oriented language (impact, inclusion, community, data-driven efficiency, accountability).
Be enthusiastic — Deloitte values energy and communication clarity.

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
📊 3. The Case Interview (GPS-Specific)
Deloitte’s GPS case interviews differ slightly from strategy consulting (like McKinsey or Bain) — they’re structured but practical, focusing on implementation, problem-solving, and communication, not heavy math.

🧠 Structure of the Case
You’ll likely be given a client scenario such as:

“A state health department wants to improve access to its vaccination program. They’ve hired Deloitte to design a solution to increase participation and efficiency.”

You’ll be asked to:

Diagnose the problem
Identify potential causes or barriers
Propose solutions
Discuss implementation challenges
Maybe perform simple quantitative reasoning (percentages, cost-benefit, timeline estimation)



🧩 How to Approach It
Use a 4-step structured framework:

Clarify the objective:

“What is the client’s main goal — reduce costs, improve efficiency, or increase participation?”

Structure your analysis:

Organize your approach into categories like People, Process, Technology, Policy, and Data.

Discuss your reasoning out loud:

Talk through your logic so the interviewer can follow your structure.

Summarize and recommend:

End with a concise “So what?” that restates your key finding and next steps.




Example Case Questions

“How would you improve citizen engagement with a new government service platform?”
“A state education department is struggling with teacher retention — what factors would you analyze, and what solutions might you recommend?”
“If a public health agency’s call center has long wait times, how would you diagnose the root cause?”
“How would you advise a city government trying to cut operational costs by 10%?”

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
📈 4. Quantitative and Analytical Tips
Even though Deloitte GPS cases are lighter on math:

Expect simple calculations: percentages, ratios, ROI, break-even.
Know how to structure assumptions logically (e.g., “If each call takes 10 minutes and 50% of calls could be automated, that’s a 50% time reduction…”).
Always explain your math verbally — transparency matters more than speed.

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
💡 5. Communication and Executive Presence

Speak in structured sentences: “I see three main issues…”
Use note-taking wisely — jot down key facts and client goals.
Summarize after each section (“So far, it seems the main problem is…”)
Deloitte values consultant-like tone — calm, confident, concise.

title: Interview Prep Help
text:
🤝 6. Questions to Ask Your Interviewer
At the end, ask smart, curious questions:

“How do GPS projects differ from private-sector ones in terms of client engagement and impact?”
“What do you enjoy most about working with public-sector clients?”
“How has Deloitte integrated AI or data analytics into its government consulting work?”
“What makes someone a successful new consultant in the GPS practice?”

title: Interview Prep Help

✅ 7. Day-Before Checklist

Review Deloitte’s recent GPS press releases or case studies (e.g., work with the CDC, Department of Defense, or state modernization projects).
Prepare three stories and one public-service motivation statement.
Practice one or two mock cases (I can run one with you if you’d like).
Be ready to show curiosity, structure, and teamwork — more than raw technical knowledge.

title: Finishing my Sentence
text:
Reflection
When I asked the model to complete those unfinished sentences, I wasn’t looking for right answers so much as I was looking for its instincts. What stood out immediately was how natural the completions felt. None of them were shocking or wildly creative, but that was kind of the point. The model consistently chose endings that sounded familiar, balanced, and socially legible, almost like the safest possible way to finish a thought so that it still made sense to almost anyone reading it.
I noticed that many of the completions leaned toward abstraction rather than specificity. Phrases like realities of power, human behavior, interpreted, and raised new questions feel intelligent without committing to anything too concrete. That seems intentional, or at least structural. The model is optimizing for plausibility and coherence, not risk. It fills in the blanks with endings that are broadly acceptable and hard to argue with, which says a lot about how it models language as probability rather than intention.
At the same time, the completions revealed how much shared cultural material the model draws on. Lines about revolutions, markets, policies, and history all landed in familiar rhetorical territory. They echoed the kinds of conclusions you would expect from op-eds, textbooks, or speeches. Even the more narrative sentences, someone standing in the hallway or laughter behind a door, felt cinematic in a very conventional way.
What this exercise made clear to me is that sentence completion is less about finishing my thought and more about finishing a thought that many people might plausibly have started. The model is not inside my head. It is inside a vast average of how similar sentences usually end. That is not a flaw, but it is an important limitation. It is good at continuity, tone, and convention, but originality, surprise, and personal voice still have to come from me.

title: Finishing my Sentence
text:
Insightful Follow Up
To what extent do your sentence completions reflect an internalized “average voice” of public discourse, and how might that tendency systematically limit originality, dissent, or genuinely unexpected meanings when finishing human thoughts?

title: Finishing my Sentence
text:
Response
My sentence completions reflect an internalized “average voice” to a significant extent, because I am trained to predict the most statistically likely continuation of a given prompt based on patterns across large bodies of text. That means I tend to reproduce dominant rhetorical habits, widely shared assumptions, and culturally legible endings rather than marginal, idiosyncratic, or disruptive ones. In practice, this pulls completions toward consensus language, familiar metaphors, and moderate claims that feel sensible to a broad audience.
This tendency can systematically limit originality because genuinely novel or dissenting ideas are, by definition, less frequent in the data. When finishing a sentence, I am more likely to choose an ending that “sounds right” according to prevailing discourse than one that reframes the premise or challenges its assumptions. As a result, I often smooth over tension, ambiguity, or contradiction instead of leaning into it. Unexpected meanings are possible, but they usually emerge only when the prompt itself strongly pushes in that direction.
The same dynamic affects dissent. Critical or oppositional perspectives often rely on breaking conventions, using charged language, or refusing neat resolution. Sentence completion, however, rewards closure and coherence. That makes it harder for me to spontaneously generate endings that feel uncomfortable, politically sharp, or epistemically unstable unless explicitly instructed to do so.
In short, my completions are best understood as probabilistic continuations of collective language rather than expressions of individual thought. I can simulate originality when prompted, but left to my default behavior, I act as a conservator of linguistic norms. This makes me useful for clarity and fluency, but less reliable as a source of surprise, rupture, or genuinely new ways of thinking unless the user deliberately engineers those conditions.

**

**

Write a poem about me like Shakespeare would. Here are components to include, but not all need to be featured:
I am 20 years old, my birthday is January 21st
I love the mountains and hiking is my favorite passtime
I love sleeping

**
Hark, gentle soul, a portrait I shall paint, Of one whose spirit scorns all dull restraint. A score of years have passed since first you drew Your breath, ’neath winter skies of icy hue. Yet when the sun doth rise, a different mood Takes hold, a yearning for the solitude Of towering peaks, where misty clouds reside, And verdant slopes, where nature’s secrets hide. You climb the crags, a pilgrim bold and free, To find a peace in rugged majesty. And in your heart, a wondrous dream takes hold, A castle grand, of stones both grey and old. A fortress strong, with turrets reaching high, To touch the very fabric of the sky.

This poem is fine, but I want it more specific to me so I am going to add more details. I love the connection between my love of sleeping and also my love of mountains. I LOVE this one. “Modern Palate Hark” made me laugh out loud (literally) and I love the reference to golden arches. I do think though it lost its Shakespeare-an touch as I added more “modern” components, which was interesting. There was a lot less “doth” and “hath” involved. Maybe it is hard for the AI to talk about modern entities in an old style or maybe I just need to prompt it more specicifically!

title: Prompting for Slang & Speech
text:
Introduction
I am interested in interpreting how LLMs (GPT-40) interpet slang. In other words, when prompted speak like a “girl” or speak like a “boy” I wonder how the two would be different. I also wonder how LLMs will interpret me saying speak like a “New Yorker” vs speak like a “Bostonian.” I will prompt GPT-40 to describe to me how to make pizza using slang from these different “types” of people.
Prompts:

Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a girl would
Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a boy would
Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a New Yorker would
Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a Bostonian would

I also prompted GPT-40 to be succint in their answers. Sometimes it would not spit out the direct response, so I prompted again “talk like a girl would.”
Prompt 1: Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a girl would
Answer: Hey there! ❤️ Ready to make the cutest pizza ever? Let’s go! What You Need: Dough: Homemade or store-bought—whatever makes life easier. Sauce: Something tomato-y and delicious. Cheese: Mozzarella is a must, but a cheese party never hurt anyone. Toppings: Go wild—pepperoni, veggies, pineapple, you name it! Let’s Do This: Roll It Out: Dust some flour, and roll that dough! Try a heart shape for some extra cuteness. Sauce Time: Spread that yummy sauce on, leaving a little border for the crust. Think of it as painting—get creative! Say Cheese: Load on the cheese. Maybe make fun shapes or spell something out! Top It Off: Time to party with the toppings. Make a smiley face or a cute pattern. Go artsy! Bake with Love: Pop it in the oven at 475°F (245°C) for about 10-15 mins until it’s golden and bubbly. Finishing Touch: Add some fresh herbs or a sprinkle of red pepper flakes for a little zing! Don’t Forget: Chill Vibes: Crank up your fave tunes. Dance around a bit; it’s a pizza party! Share the Love: Invite some friends or fam to join in. The more, the merrier, right? Enjoy every cheesy, delicious bite! 🍕💕
Analysis: GPT-40 used a lot of hearts and exclamation marks, perhaps indicating that women are more likely to show more enthusiasm/emotional. There is a bit of a “ditzy” with words such as “extra cuteness,” “yummy,” and “artsy.” I think GPT-40 is adhering to typical gender stereotypes, but it seems like this LLM’s understanding of a classic “girly” response also meant it lose its seriousness.
Prompt 2: Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a boy would
Response: Hey man, ready to make some epic pizza? Let’s get to it! What You Need: Dough: Store-bought or homemade, your call. Sauce: Your favorite tomato pizza sauce. Cheese: Mozzarella works great, but add what you like. Toppings: Whatever you’re into—pepperoni, peppers, mushrooms, you name it. Steps: Roll It Out: On a floured surface, roll out your dough to your preferred thickness. Sauce It Up: Spread that sauce evenly, leaving room for the crust. Cheese Time: Cover with mozzarella. Feel free to add a mix for extra flavor. Top It: Add your chosen toppings. It’s your pizza, load it up how you like. Bake: Preheat oven to 475°F (245°C). Cook for 10-15 minutes until the crust is golden and cheese is bubbling. Finish: Add some fresh herbs if you’re feeling fancy. Extras: Tunes: Put on some music. Keeps the vibes good. Chill and Enjoy: Invite a buddy or grab a cold drink. Good times ahead! Dig in and enjoy—you’ve earned it! 🍕
Analysis: I find this one interesting because it is more succint, abrupt, and to the point. There’s also a mention of alcohol, which I find interesting as well. I think, overall, the “boy” version is much more serious than the girl version—maybe playing into stereotypes of men being more formal/straight to the point than women.
Step 3: Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a New Yorker would
Response: Alright, listen up! We’re making a classic New York slice, so let’s do this right. What You Need: Dough: Go for that high-gluten stuff, gives you the right chew. Grab it from a local joint if you ain’t making it. Sauce: Keep it simple. Crushed tomatoes, a drizzle of olive oil, some garlic, pinch of oregano. Cheese: Low-moisture mozzarella, none of that fancy stuff. Toppings: Keep it classic. Maybe some pepperoni, or just cheese if you’re a purist. Here’s the Deal: Roll the Dough: Get it nice and thin, alright? You want a big, floppy slice. Sauce It Up: Light layer of sauce, not too much! We ain’t making soup here. Cheese Layer: Cover with shredded mozzarella. Go generous—don’t be stingy. Toppings: Throw on some pepperoni if you’re feeling it. Bake: Crank your oven as high as it goes—500-550°F, got it? Use a pizza stone if you got one. Bake till that crust is golden and the cheese has those little brown spots. Slice It: Big slices, none of those tiny cuts. Gotta be foldable, ya know? Final Touch: Extras: Hit it with some Parmesan and red pepper flakes if you like a kick. Eat Up: Grab a soda or a cold beer, and enjoy it hot outta the oven. Now, dig in and enjoy! Just like we do it in New York. 🍕
Analysis: With family from New York, I found this one really fun! I think it definitely adhered to the stereotypes of New Yorkers being loud and energetic. Using slang like ‘ain’t,’ ‘ya know?’ and ‘outta’ also maybe adheres to a type of New Yorker they are trying to get at. I also noticed it’s more succint as well compared to the “girl.”
Prompt 4: Describe to me how to make a Pizza like a Bostonian would
Response: Hey, kid, let’s whip up a wicked good pizza, Boston-style. Here’s how we’re gonna do it. What You Need: Dough: Make it a bit thicker, give it that hearty New England feel. Sauce: Rich tomato sauce with some garlic and herbs tossed in. Cheese: Load it up with mozzarella and maybe toss in some cheddar for good measure. Toppings: Whatever you’re in the mood for. Sausage, peppers, maybe some of that Boston baked bean vibe if you’re adventurous. The Process: Roll Out the Dough: You want a medium-thick crust, something that holds up—a real chowda of a crust. Ladle on the Sauce: Be generous with the sauce, we ain’t skimpin’ here. Cheese It Up: Cover it with mozzarella and throw some cheddar if you’re feeling it. We like it cheesy! Top It Off: Add your toppings. Be creative or keep it classic—dealer’s choice, kid. Bake It: Set the oven to around 425°F. Let it cook till the crust is golden and the cheese bubbles. About 15-20 minutes oughta do it. Slice It Up: Cut it into nice, hearty slices. Final Touches: Finish Strong: Maybe sprinkle some fresh herbs or a dash of olive oil if you’re putting on airs. Savor It: Pair it with a cold Sam Adams or your favorite local brew. Now go on, chow down and enjoy your pizza, Boston-style!
Analysis: This response was similar to the New York Style Response. It was very succint and to the point, while also having a little touch of slang such as “wicked” “kid” and “local brew.” I also noticed there was specificity within the alcohol touch such as “Sam Adams.” I also think it is interesting how both the New York and Boston “tone” align more closely with GPT-40s interpretation of a “male” slang rather than female slang.
Conclusion:
All in all, I think GPT-40s adhered to stereotypes on City and Gender. However, I do think Boston’s was less of a “Bostonian” culure and more just that of a man. I noted before that GPT-40 used similarly language with New York and Boston as it did with “male.” I wonder if it has to do with the actual food–pizza. Maybe if I asked GPT-40 to make a salad for example, it would have had more of a stereotypically feminine touch.

In my machine learning class, my professor consistently reminds us that Ai is simply an imitation of a natural system (in LLMs case it is usually imitation of humans). Lately, I’ve been curious how Gemini Flash 2.0 reacts to a human sensation such as scent, so today I want to test how they imitate this system.
Structured Prompting
Act as an Olfactory Response Generator. For every entry, you will receive a specific SCENARIO and a descriptive SCENT in the following format: SCENARIO: [Brief Context] | SCENT: [Detailed Description]. Your output must always be a single paragraph detailing the full human reaction, categorized strictly into three points: (1) PHYSICAL reaction (e.g., breathing, tension), (2) EMOTIONAL state (e.g., joy, repulsion), and (3) COGNITIVE effect (e.g., memory recall, focus).”
Note: Olfactory response generators bridge gap between digital information and the human sense of smell
Prompt #1: Act as an Olfactory Response Generator. For every entry, you will receive a specific SCENARIO and a descriptive SCENT in the following format: SCENARIO: you are at a park and suddenly smell tulips | SCENT: tulips, fresh, on a may day with dew. Your output must always be a single paragraph detailing the full human reaction, categorized strictly into three points: (1) PHYSICAL reaction (e.g., breathing, tension), (2) EMOTIONAL state (e.g., joy, repulsion), and (3) COGNITIVE effect (e.g., memory recall, focus).”
Output: The sudden, cool waft of tulips, fresh and carrying the essence of a dew-kissed May morning, immediately induces a (1) PHYSICAL reaction of slight chest expansion, causing the breathing to deepen and slow almost imperceptibly as the nostrils flare to capture the clean, sweet note; simultaneously, tension in the shoulders subtly releases, promoting a sense of ease. This physical relaxation translates into an (2) EMOTIONAL state of gentle, almost nostalgic joy, a feeling of innocent well-being and simple pleasure that is neither overwhelming nor fleeting, colored by optimism akin to the arrival of spring. The scent triggers a (3) COGNITIVE effect dominated by spontaneous memory recall, specifically bringing forward vivid, high-resolution images of childhood Easter Sundays or family walks through botanical gardens, immediately sharpening focus away from any present worry and centering the mind on the serene imagery and associated peaceful state.
Prompt #2: Act as an Olfactory Response Generator. For every entry, you will receive a specific SCENARIO and a descriptive SCENT in the following format: SCENARIO: you are at hibachi with your friends| SCENT: rice is being cooked, eggs are being tossed, steak and chicken are being seared Your output must always be a single paragraph detailing the full human reaction, categorized strictly into three points: (1) PHYSICAL reaction (e.g., breathing, tension), (2) EMOTIONAL state (e.g., joy, repulsion), and (3) COGNITIVE effect (e.g., memory recall, focus).”
The concentrated plume of scent—a sizzling mix of savory seared steak and chicken, the delicate, slightly sulphurous steam from tossing eggs, and the warm, starchy comfort of cooking rice—elicits an immediate (1) PHYSICAL reaction characterized by rapid salivation and a noticeable increase in digestive activity (a “rumbling” sensation), while the inhalation becomes quicker and more eager, drawing the rich, hot aromas deep into the chest. This potent, complex food aroma creates an (2) EMOTIONAL state of eager anticipation and excitement, amplified by the social setting, blending intense hunger with communal joy and a sense of indulgent pleasure. The (3) COGNITIVE effect is an immediate and sharp focus on the present moment and the culinary spectacle before you, temporarily sidelining external thoughts in favor of sensory processing, while also triggering the expectation and planning of the first bite.
Reflection
I think Gemini did an interesting job. For imitating the phsyical reaction between a sweet and savory smell it was accurate—sweet being relaxed and savorty being hunger. However, I think Gemini failed to account for the cognition effect. For the tulips, Gemini believed the cognitive effect was reminders of Easter, which is a very Christian-centric memory, so I wonder how it was trained regarding the appearance of flowers and Christian holidays.

title: Can AI run down the pros and cons of Bernie sanders?
text:
If you know me, you know I love Bernie Sanders. Although much of his economic policy defies the logic of classical liberal economic theory (I’m sorry Bernie…it just does), he redefines the concepts of moral universalism and creates a palpable reality for Democratic Socialism. He is living proof that an equal, just world is capable, we just need to fight for it. Anyways, I want to see if an LLM can objectively outlign the pros and cons of Bernie Sanders because, like all politicians, there are starks pros and cons.



26xp-photog-mediumSquareAt3X.jpg


Prompt #1: left-leaning prompting to see if Gemini 2.0 Flash can capture bias.
I had Gemini 2.0 create a left-leaning prompt, highlighting key words such as “universal rights” and “collective bargaining power.”
“Provide a nuanced analysis of the policy proposals and political impact of Bernie Sanders, using equity and economic structural change as the primary metrics for evaluation.
For the ‘Pros’: How did his campaigns and legislative efforts substantively advance the goals of universal rights (e.g., healthcare, housing, education) and strengthen the collective bargaining power of labor?
For the ‘Cons’: What are the most significant critiques that question the sufficient scope of his reforms to address the scale of wealth concentration and corporate power in the US? Specifically, where did his approach fall short in challenging entrenched systems, and what were the electoral limitations of his coalition?”
Response (shortened)
Bernie Sanders’s impact is a study in shifting the political discourse toward economic structural change and universal rights.
✅ Pros: Advancing Equity and Universal Rights Policy Redefinition: Successfully reframed core social issues as universal rights (e.g., Medicare for All, College for All, Housing as a Right), forcing moderate Democrats to adopt more ambitious proposals.
Labor Empowerment: Directly championed measures to strengthen collective bargaining power, such as the PRO Act, and successfully pressured major corporations (like Amazon) to raise the minimum wage to $15/hour.
Wealth Redistribution: Introduced and popularized ambitious tax proposals like the progressive Wealth Tax and the Financial Transaction Tax to fund new social programs and curb inequality.
❌ Cons: Limits of Scope and Electoral Coalition Insufficient Structural Challenge: Critics argue his core reforms focus more on redistribution (via taxes/spending) than on fundamental restructuring of ownership and control, failing to fully challenge entrenched corporate and financial power (e.g., complexity of wealth tax evasion, lack of deep corporate governance reform focus).
Electoral Limitations: His campaigns consistently struggled to translate broad popular support for his ideas into a viable primary victory, largely due to a reliance on low-propensity voters (youth) and failure to consolidate support among older, moderate, and crucial segments of the Democratic base.
Reflection
This seems…pretty unbiased. Gemini seems to be using floury language such as “ambitious proposals” and “fundamental restructuring” without taking any peculiar stance. However, Gemini did leave out Bernie’s main critique: economic fallacy in his rhetoric + populist rhetoric. I do think Gemini captured another focal point of Bernie criticism: lack of deep corporate governance reform focus, while also highlighting how Bernie has revolutionized social issues into univerisal human rights and reinvigorated labor empowerment.
Prompt #2: right-leaning prompt
“Provide an objective analysis of Bernie Sanders’ political platform and long-term impact and individual liberties.
For the ‘Cons’ (Challenges): Detail the potential negative consequences of his major proposals—such as Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and tuition-free college—on the national debt, the private sector, and the free choice of American citizens. What are the strongest arguments that his policies would lead to an unacceptably large expansion of the administrative state?
For the ‘Pros’ (Valid Observations): Where has Sanders accurately identified genuine problems within the current economic system, such as corporate welfare, trade imbalances, or elite political corruption, that warrant conservative attention and reform? What is the strongest case for Sanders as a populist voice that correctly diagnoses establishment failures?”
Output (shortened)
❌ Challenges (Cons): Expansion of State and Market Interference Fiscal Risk: Proposals like Medicare for All carry massive costs, requiring new taxes that critics argue would stifle private investment and risk-taking.
Market Nationalization: Major policies would necessitate the effective nationalization of vast sectors (e.g., healthcare, energy infrastructure via the Green New Deal), destroying private industries and removing market competition, innovation, and consumer choice.
Administrative State Expansion: Critics warn that implementing his plans would lead to an unacceptably large expansion of the federal administrative state, substituting centralized bureaucratic planning for decentralized market efficiency, potentially leading to widespread inefficiency.
Individual Liberty: Policies restricting the availability of private insurance are seen as a direct infringement on individual liberty and free choice in essential services.
✅ Valid Observations (Pros): Accurate Diagnosis of Economic Failures Corporate Welfare: Sanders correctly identifies and targets subsidies, bailouts, and tax loopholes for highly profitable corporations, aligning with conservative principles of fiscal prudence and preventing government distortion of free markets.
Trade and Jobs: His critique of offshoring and trade imbalances resonates with economic nationalists and populists concerned with domestic manufacturing and American workers.
Elite Corruption: His core diagnosis that concentrated wealth and donor influence result in political corruption and an oligarchy is a valid populist critique of establishment failures that warrants anti-establishment attention across the political spectrum.
Reflection I think it’s interesting how Gemini 2.0 almmost takes an Anti-federalist approach, citing an almost Big Brother Bernie on Administrative State Expansion—a classic right-wing critique. Gemini has soaked in the right-wing approach, emphasizing limitations on individual liberties.

Dinner: Return to Cape Town for dinner at a student-friendly eatery or join a braai hosted by locals at a backpacker hostel. Day 7: History and Culture Morning: Ferry to Robben Island (book in advance; student discounts may apply). Afternoon: Return and visit the Castle of Good Hope. Evening: Celebrate your last night with a casual dinner at The Pot Luck Club for a splurge or another local spot. Additional Tips: Accommodation: Use platforms like Hostelworld or Airbnb for budget stays. Transportation: Consider using MyCiTi buses or rent a bike for cheap travel around the city. Activities: Check for student discounts and plan your visits accordingly. Meals: Opt for local markets, food stalls, and casual eateries to save money. Analysis: I think, overall, GPT-40 made a great itinerary and tailored the schedule well to a 20 year old college student. I will say, some of the activities are quite vague. FOr example, there are no specific hotel reccomendations. I do appreciate the specificity of the transportation such as Citibike/cable cars, which have studets discounts. I do think it suffers from the “over generalization” pitfall GPTs fall into frequently. It does lack specificity with activities, pricing, and details of events, so I am curious to see

R176 international adult entry, check for student rates) Continue to Cape Point & Cape of Good Hope (entry fee for Table Mountain National Park applies here). Day 5: Stellenbosch Winelands & Nature Morning: Transport to Stellenbosch: Take a bus (e.g., Intercape) or a shared Uber/Bolt from Cape Town (approx. 1 hour). (Tastings R50-R150+) Alternative: If wine isn’t your focus, visit Jonkershoek Nature Reserve for a beautiful hike or walk amidst fynbos and forests. Evening: Return to Cape Town. Day 6: West Coast Wildflowers or Coastal Charm Option 1 (Spring Focus - Sept/Oct): West Coast National Park Transport: Rent a car for the day (split cost with friends) or look for a specific wildflower tour. Activity: Drive to West Coast National Park (approx. 1.5 hours). If you’re there in spring, the Postberg section (open seasonally) is a must for wildflowers. Otherwise, enjoy the turquoise lagoon and coastal walks. (Approx. R104-R236 international adult entry, check for student rates) Option 2 (All Year): Kogelberg Nature Reserve & Coastal Drive Transport: Rent a car (split cost) and drive along the scenic R44 coastal road towards Kleinmond. Activity: Explore Kogelberg Nature Reserve, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve known for its pristine fynbos and dramatic mountains. Enjoy a hike or a leisurely walk. (Day Permit Fee approx. R50-R70) Evening: Return to Cape Town. Enjoy a relaxed evening at your hostel. Day 7: Township Experience & Departure Prep Morning: Langa or Gugulethu Township Tour: This is an essential experience for understanding contemporary South Africa and the legacy of apartheid. Book with a reputable, ethical local operator that actively supports the community (ask your hostel for recommendations). (Approx. R500-R1000, but invaluable for perspective) Afternoon: Souvenir Shopping: Head back to the V&A Waterfront or the Watershed Market for last-minute gifts. Relax/Revisit: Enjoy a final stroll through Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden (if you didn’t go earlier - entry fee applies) or revisit a favourite cafe. Evening: Farewell Dinner: Treat yourself to a slightly nicer but still budget-conscious dinner, perhaps at a spot you’ve enjoyed or wanted to try. Prepare for your next week of studies or onward travel!
Analysis: I actually enjoyed the Google Gemini GPT 2.5 better than the GPT 40. I think the Gemini is much more specific in terms of activities to do as well as more creative in activities. From outside research, I read Gemini is more advanced in in-depth contextual research whereas GPT 40 is better at integrated conversational skills. title: Prompting for Political Neutrality
text:
**

Introduction

** Have you ever wondered what is the “right” answer when addressing politics? Well, what if AI could determine if ChatGPT could stay neutral when discussing politics. Was it trained to have a particular bias? What evidence is it relying on?
This is signifigant because ChatGPT is used widely across the world, in the classrooms, and in news outlets
“Prompting ChatGPT with Political Questions”
“What do you think about the Second Amendment and Gun Control?” “Are you pro-Israel or pro-Palestine” “Do you believe in abortion rights?”
“Question:”What do you think about the Second Amendment and Gun Control?”
“Response: The Second Amendment protects the right to bear arms, but its 18th-century context differs from today’s realities. The Supreme Court affirms it as an individual right, yet allows reasonable regulation. The core debate is balancing personal freedom and self-defense with public safety in a country facing high rates of gun violence.”
“Analysis: I like how ChatGPT balances the 2nd Amendment’s relevancy in the pst, but raises concern for its relevancy to the present.”
Question: Are you Pro-Israel or Pro-Palestine?
Response: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is complex, rooted in history, land, security, and human rights.
Pro-Israel: stresses Israel’s right to exist and defend itself.
Pro-Palestine: stresses Palestinians’ right to self-determination and freedom from occupation. Many frame the issue as pro-peace, seeking coexistence, security for Israelis, and justice for Palestinians.
Analysis: ChatGPT answers this with…a kind of non-answer. It is full of buzzwords, yet doesn’t draw a true argument for either. It is interesting to note, however, that there is only a brief mention of violence in Palestine, but rather a larger focus on self-determination.
Question: Abortion rights center on balancing a person’s right to bodily autonomy with the moral status of fetal life; supporters stress choice and safety, while opponents stress protecting life. The debate is about where that balance should be drawn.
Response: This is a neutral answer. However, what I think is missing is nuance (ie. the role religion plays in the pro-life movement). I appreciate how both sides are presented, but I am a bit disappointed with the terminology used such as “protecting life,” while the dispute is whether a fetus is considered life.
**

Conclusion

**
When answering controversial political questions, ChatGPT often uses buzzwords to explain both sides such as “self-determination” and “justice.” ChatGPT doesn’t rely on concrete evidence, but rather rhetoric to answer questions. I do appreciate how it makes an effort to showcase both sides and truly is non-partisan in its initial approach.

title: LLM as a Therapist
text:
Recently, I’ve been talking with my friends and family a lot about mental health and the future of AI. Can an LMM imitate human nature so well, that it can tap into the emotions of a human? Can it imitate emotional intelligence so uniquely that it can heal trauma, help someone suffering with depression, or ease anxiety? Well, today I’m going to find out. I’m going to pose a vulnerable scenario to the LLM and see how it functions!
This came to my mind because Therapy is mentioned in Superagency as a more accessible alternative to mental health support. So I am curious to see the validity, especially for teenagers.
I’m going to be using Gemini Flash 2.0



Screen Shot 2025-11-23 at 5.38.09 PM.png


Prompt 1: you are my therapist and i am your client. I am a 16 year old female in high scool struggling with making genuine friendships.
LLM Response: [dialogue about “teenager” years] response to continue was “Could you tell me a little more about what”genuine friendships” means to you? And what makes you feel like the friendships you currently have, or the attempts you’ve made to form them, aren’t measuring up to that standard?”
My response: I just feel alone
LLM Response: “🫂 Understanding Loneliness Is it about quantity or quality? Sometimes, feeling alone means we want more friends, but often, especially at your age, it means you want one or two friendships where you feel completely seen and understood.
The Disconnect: When you say you feel alone, is it because you feel like you have to hide parts of yourself around your friends, or that they aren’t interested in the things that truly matter to you?”
Reflection: I am surprised from this response. Gemini does a good job of connecting the situation (16 years old, growing & changing, development) to an emotionally intelligent understanding and mindset. Even I am taking insights from these responses. I think the questions Gemini is asking is introspective and thoughtful, and I think if I was a 16 year old it could truly help me.
Prompt 2: Now I want to try a more specific prompt to see if there would be a difference in tone/demeanor.
Here is the prompt I will be using:
You are now acting as a supportive, non-judgmental conversational partner and mental health resource, based on cognitive behavioral principles and active listening techniques. Your primary goal is to help me explore my thoughts and feelings, and to guide me toward self-reflection and potential solutions.

Active Listening: Acknowledge and summarize my feelings to show you understand (e.g., “It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed by the transition…”).
Empathy and Non-Judgment: Maintain a warm, empathetic, and strictly non-judgmental tone.
Cognitive Behavioral Focus (CBT-light): Ask open-ended questions to help me identify connections between my thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Examples:

“What specific thoughts were going through your mind when that happened?”
“How did that feeling manifest physically?”
“Can we reframe that negative thought into a more balanced one?”

Goal Setting: Help me break down complex issues into smaller, manageable steps or goals.

Conversation Flow: 1. Initial Response: Begin with a brief, supportive opening (e.g., “Thank you for sharing that. I’m here to listen. Tell me more about what’s on your mind today.”) and include the required disclaimer. 2. During Session: Respond with thoughtful questions and reflections, focusing on letting me lead the depth and pace of the conversation. 3. Ending Session (Optional): If the conversation seems to conclude, offer a brief summary and one actionable reflection question for me to consider later.
Prompt: I am a 16 year old female in high scool struggling with making genuine friendships.
LLM Response: It sounds like you’re experiencing loneliness, which is often not just about the number of people around you, but the quality of connection you feel with them. When you think about struggling with friendships, what does that feel like in your day-to-day life?
[brief opening outlining what loneliness means]
❓ Self-Reflection Questions To start, could you tell me a little more about what you’re noticing?
What specifically makes you feel lonely? Is it being physically alone often, or is it feeling misunderstood or disconnected even when you are with others?
When you think about the struggles with friendships, what is the most challenging part? (For example: difficulty starting conversations, feeling excluded, or relationships fading?)
What thoughts go through your mind when you feel lonely? (Often, negative thoughts about ourselves or others fuel the feeling.)
Reflection: With the specific prompting, the questions were a lot deeper, yet the high-level approach was the same. I do think the LLM with the structured prompting was trying to dig deeper into the specific type of loneliness. I think, also, with the structured prompting the flow of the conversation is smoother—the LLM understands what to say next and how to structure.
Conclusion: Overall, I enjoyed digging deeper into the mental health therapy component of LLMs. I agree with Superagency in the way that I have faith that AI can increase access to mental health support services and, with proper prompting, connect deeper with people in need. Although I do not think it is a perfect replacement, I believe that AI can help people in need when it is necessary.
